extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, literary critics, and readers of aesthetics/philosophy of art
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for creating and evaluating poetry, allegory, and tragic drama, with comparisons to plastic/pictorial art and history; covers forms (lyric, ballad, epic, drama), devices (allegory, metaphor, epithet), and modes of introducing misfortune in tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory in plastic and pictorial art
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory is foreign to the end of plastic and pictorial art and often interferes with it; such arts 'devote themselves to the perception, and therefore it is æsthetical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using allegory as the primary aim in painting or sculpture because it leads away from what is perceptibly given (the proper object of these arts) toward abstract thoughts. If an artwork presents an arbitrary connection between what is depicted and an abstract significance, it has passed into mere symbolism with attendant disadvantages (e.g., meaning may be forgotten and the image become 'dumb').

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory in poetry (permissible and serviceable)
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, allegory is permissible and very serviceable because poetry's immediate material is conception (abstract thought), and it may lead from this to the representation of perceptible objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use allegory, metaphor, simile, parable to make abstract conceptions perceptible by calling up images for the hearer's imagination. Pictorial execution is secondary—an allegorical picture accompanying a poem need only represent the thing so it can be recognised. Examples: Cervantes' comparison of sleep to a mantle, Plato's Cave, Gracian's Criticon, Don Quixote and Gulliver's Travels as concealed allegories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish symbol from poetical allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: A symbol rests on an agreement and can become unintelligible when its conventional meaning is forgotten; a poetical allegory intends to make an abstract conception perceptible via representative image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer allegory that makes the Idea perceptible over arbitrary symbols whose meaning requires prior agreement or a translator (e.g., the fish as a Christian symbol is opaque without learned explanation). Beware that symbolic conventions may decay and render the work mute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of poetry: revelation of the Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of poetry is the revelation of the Ideas (grades of the objectification of will) and the communication of them to the hearer with distinctness and vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange abstract conceptions so their spheres intersect and precipitate a perceptible representative for the imagination; the poet must make the Idea knowable by perception—the knowledge of the Idea is the end of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epithets to narrow universality toward perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Epithets in poetry serve to narrow the universality of a concept until it becomes perceptible (the poet 'precipitates' the concrete out of abstract universality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply descriptive adjectives that intersect and diminish the concept's sphere to bring it nearer to sensory perception (example: Homer's frequent adjectival attachments to substantives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and rhyme as perceptual aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm and rhyme are powerful aids because our faculties of perception are bound to time; they hold attention and produce a blind consent to what is read prior to judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regular recurring sound patterns to both keep the listener's attention and to give the poem an emphatic persuasive power independent of argumentative reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic material and range
rubrics_metrics.description: Because poetry uses concepts as its material, its province is very great: the whole of nature and Ideas of all grades can be represented; representations may be descriptive, narrative, or dramatic according to the Idea to be imparted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the form (description, narrative, drama) appropriate to the Idea you aim to reveal; poetry can address both low and high grades of objectivity depending on poetic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs history: inner (ideal) truth vs phenomenal truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry comprehends the Idea (inner nature of man outside time) and therefore often offers a truer inner truth than history, which apprehends phenomena in relation and consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating truthfulness regarding the 'nature of man,' give weight to poetic representation of Ideas for inner, universal insight; recognize that history's method (following particular data and causes) limits it to phenomenal truth and often introduces factual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, fidelity, and plausibility in poetic representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute truth (faithfulness) is a necessary condition of poetic effect; lack of unity in characters, contradiction of character or of human nature, impossibility, or great improbability in events offend poetry much as technical faults offend painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters are internally consistent, actions plausible within the world of the poem, and avoid contradictions or impossible occurrences even in accessories; think of poetic fidelity as a 'faithful mirror of life' but clarified and arranged for significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant characters and pregnant situations
rubrics_metrics.description: In romance, epic, and drama the revelation of the Idea is principally attained by (1) true and profound representation of significant characters, and (2) invention of pregnant situations in which they disclose themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and design characters and situations so that the characters' peculiar qualities unfold fully and distinctly; manufacture or select circumstances that force those qualities to display themselves (analogous to exposing chemical elements to revealing reagents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of circumstances to disclose an Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: To comprehend fully the Ideas of something (e.g., water), it must be shown under varied circumstances and obstacles; likewise, for human Ideas, varied situations reveal different qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose characters/themes to diverse conditions (conflict, constraint, chance, extremes) so their essential traits and the Idea they exemplify become apparent—avoid static or single-moment depictions when the Idea requires variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as highest poetical art (representation of the terrible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the summit of poetical art because its end is the representation of the terrible side of life: unspeakable pain, triumph of evil, scornful mastery of chance, and the irretrievable fall of the just and innocent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In tragedy aim to reveal the strife of will with itself through suffering that leads to heightened knowledge or resignation; tragic effect should culminate in purification or renunciation (e.g., hero dies purified or surrenders the will), not in satisfying poetic justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject demand for poetical justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand for so-called poetical justice is a misconception about tragedy and about the nature of the world; tragedy's point is not moral retribution but deeper metaphysical insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require that dramatic outcomes restore moral balance; instead allow tragedy to show suffering and fall as revealing of the human condition and the 'crime of existence' itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of introducing misfortune in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Misfortune in tragedy may be introduced by (1) a character of extraordinary wickedness who causes it, (2) blind fate (chance and error), or (3) the mere relations/position of the dramatis personae that compel mutual harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the third mode (misfortune arising from ordinary characters placed in tragic relations) as the most powerful: it makes misfortune seem essential and near by showing how ordinary people, in certain relational positions, can produce the greatest harm without monstrous character or rare accident. Examples: Richard III/Iago/Shylock (first), Oedipus (second), Romeo and Juliet (second/third), etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric poetry: subjectivity and alternation with pure perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The lyric is essentially the subject of will (the singer's volition) perceived by consciousness, together with an alternation between desire (will) and moments of pure, will-less knowing; the lyrical mood expresses the mingled divided state of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose lyrics as concentrated expressions of a present emotional state that alternate between personal desire and brief contemplative perception; lyric is the most subjective and the easiest poetic form, often producible by strong momentary excitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradient of objectivity across poetic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity in poetry increases across forms: lyric is most subjective, ballad somewhat objective, idyll less subjective, romance still less, true epic almost entirely objective, drama the most objective and most difficult form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form according to degree of objectivity required: use lyric for immediate subjective states, drama for fully objective representation of characters and actions revealing Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emblems and painted fables belong to poetry's province
rubrics_metrics.description: Short painted fables with obvious morals (emblems) are to be regarded as belonging to poetry, not to painting; their pictorial execution is of secondary importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or judging emblems, emphasize the clarity of the moral/Idea rather than pictorial virtuosity; the image need only render the concept recognisable.
